ABSTRACT 
 
This research was conducted to examine the extent to which the 12th-grade 
English textbooks prepared and distributed by the two Ministries of National 
Education of both Syrian and Turkish represent ELF awareness. The research 
employed qualitative document and content analysis models. The data were 
obtained using three main theoretical frameworks: (1) Cortazzi and Jin’s (1999) 
and Yuen’s (2011) classifications of Source Culture, Target Culture, and 
International Culture, along with the 4P model (Products, Practices, 
Perspectives, Persons), for the analysis of cultural representations; (2) Matsuda’s 
(2002) classification for identifying native speaker (NS) and non-native speaker 
(NNS) representations; and (3) the strategy lists by Vettorel (2018) and Yağar 
(2020) to determine the presence of communication strategies. 
 
The findings revealed that both textbooks are inadequate in terms of ELF 
awareness. Regarding cultural representations, target culture references were 
found to be dominant in both textbooks, while source culture and international 
culture representations were quite limited. In addition, according to Yuen’s 
(2011) 4P framework, the English textbook used in Türkiye featured more 
Practices, whereas the Syrian English textbook featured more Persons. In terms 
of speakers, the Syrian English textbook included 59% non-native speakers 
(NNS), while the Turkish English textbook had 41% native speakers. Regarding 
communication strategies, rephrasing was found to be the most frequently used 
strategy in both textbooks. However, compensatory strategies (e.g., asking for 
help, using approximation, circumlocution, code-switching) were found to be 
absent from both textbooks.

CHAPTER I 
 
1. INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1. INTRODUCTION 
 
This chapter provides a systematic review of the theoretical and empirical 
literature underpinning the present research, which investigates English as a Lingua 
Franca (ELF) awareness in locally produced 12th-grade English textbooks used in 
Syrian and Turkish state high schools. The review is structured as follows. First, it 
establishes the macro-level sociolinguistic context: the historical global spread of 
English and the paradigm shift from English as a Foreign Language (EFL) to English 
as a Lingua Franca (ELF). Second, it critically examines the ideology of native-
speakerism in ELT. Third, it explores the role of ELT textbooks as ideological and 
cultural tools and details the key analytical frameworks employed in this study: 
Cortazzi and Jin's (1999) cultural typology, Yuen's (2011) 4Ps model, Matsuda's 
(2002) speaker classification, and Vettorel (2018) and Yağar's (2020) communication 
strategies. Fourth, it presents a synthesis of empirical studies from global, European, 
Turkish, Middle Eastern, Syrian, and Asian contexts. Finally, it identifies the research 
gaps that this research is designed to address. 
 
1.2. BACKGROUND OF THE RESEARCH 
 
Due to its exceptional and rapid worldwide expansion, English has become a 
global means of communication used for many purposes in political, cultural, 
financial, and educational settings across the globe (Crystal, 2003; Graddol, 1997). 
This extraordinary spread led to a significant population transition, where the number 
of non-native speakers (NNSs) of English today exceeds the number of people who 
speak it as a native language (NSs) (Bayyurt, 2018; Graddol, 2006). As a result of this 
change, English cannot be limited within the boundaries of Inner Circle countries, such 
as the United States and the United Kingdom, but has spread across the Outer and 
Expanding Circles as a global tool of communication (Kachru, 1985; Mauranen,

2012). This sociolinguistic phenomenon has changed the role of English from being a 
language of a particular nation to a lingua franca that functions as a contact 
communicative tool among people from different linguistic as well as cultural 
backgrounds for whom English is generally the only option and language medium of 
choice (Seidlhofer, 2011). 
 
Furthermore, the historical spread of English across the globe and the emergence 
of English as a lingua franca (ELF) impacted the existing traditional, monolithic 
models of Standard English and native-speaker ownership (Jenkins, 2015). According 
to the ELF perspective, language is regarded as a complicated, adaptable, and evolving 
mechanism that arises in intercultural interactions and does not adhere to native-
speaker norms (Baker, 2012; Jenkins, 2015). Thus, successful intercultural 
communication and the negotiation of meaning are more important than achieving 
native-like grammatical or phonological accuracy goals during any interaction in ELF 
(Caleffi, 2016; Matsuda, 2002). Therefore, the way that English is regarded and taught 
across the globe should critically be examined and re-evaluated, especially in settings 
where English is learned as a mandatory foreign language without any official status 
for communicative purposes worldwide (Kachru, 1985; Sifakis, 2019). 
 
However, despite this theoretical transformation in applied linguistics, English 
Language Teaching (ELT) materials, which are the primary pedagogical tools as well 
as providers of linguistic and cultural input in the classroom contexts, fall behind the 
existing sociolinguistic reality (Galloway, 2018; McGrath, 2013). Many ELT 
instructional materials that are used in ELF classrooms around the world still neglect 
the emerged diversities of English while relying on Inner Circle linguistic norms and 
providing static representations of target cultures (Syrbe & Rose, 2018; Vettorel & 
Lopriore, 2013). Thus, since the intercultural communicative competence and the 
ability to interact with other NNSs are important, some scholars within the field of 
ELF argue that such traditional materials do not adequately prepare learners for real 
life ELF interactions (Tomlinson, 2012; Yuen, 2011). 
Within contexts in the expanding circle countries like Türkiye and Syria, English 
is taught as a compulsory foreign language in state schools, and the textbooks are 
important tools used for educational purposes as well as cultural input (Bay Halil,

this research aims to identify how cultural elements (Cortazzi & Jin, 1999), NS and NNS 
(Matsuda, 2002; Syrbe & Rose, 2018), and communicatiation strategies are represented within 
these textbooks (Vettorel, 2018). 
 
1.3. STATEMENT OF THE PROBLEM 
 
Despite the fact that the English as a Lingua Franca (ELF) paradigm has been 
globally recognized and researched in applied linguistics, which also led to a 
theoretical change, Galloway (2018) argues that English language teaching materials 
still fail to reflect the new sociolinguistic phenomenon. Many studies that examined 
textbooks in terms of ELF awareness revealed that ELT materials are still based on 
native-speakerist ideology, reflecting linguistic norms and cultural representations 
from the Inner Circle without taking the diversity of global Englishes into account 
(Syrbe & Rose, 2018; Vettorel & Lopriore, 2013). This reliance on native-speakerism 
is significantly challenging the everyday subject in Expanding Circle countries. 
Jenkins (2007) states that "Several described NS English, particularly British English,

as 'original' or 'real,' and NNS Englishes as 'not real' or 'fake.'" (p. 210). Moreover, 
Galloway (2018) adds that "there is clearly a mismatch between how the language is 
actually used in today’s globalized world and the language presented in such 
materials" (p. 4). Therefore, an evaluation of ELT materials is urgently needed to 
investigate whether the shift from English as a Foreign Language (EFL) to ELF has 
been reflected in everyday teaching resources (Matsuda, 2012; Vettorel, 2018). 
 
In addition, no research was conducted to identify the origin as well as the target 
audience of ELT materials in the existing literature. Scholars in the ELF field focused 
mostly on internationally published as well as commercial coursebook resources that 
were prepared by people from countries in the Inner Circle, without paying any 
attention to state-approved materials that are designed and written by local writers 
(Guerra et al., 2022; Kopperoinen, 2011; Tajeddin & Teimournezhad, 2015). Many 
English teachers and students use locally published textbooks, which are approved by 
their ministries of education, as primary resources as well as a syllabus in contexts 
within the Expanding Circle (Bay Halil, 2019; Koçak, 2021). Thus, since "localization 
is favored by language education policymakers in their macro-planning" (Tajeddin & 
Teimournezhad, 2015, p. 1), such materials directly reflect the national ideologies of 
their countries; hence, examining them is crucial. Furthermore, McGrath (2013) 
criticizes the over-reliance on Inner Circle models in such local contexts by stating that 
"it is difficult to justify such an emphasis in materials intended for use in contexts 
where most English use is between non-native English speakers of English" (p. 9). 
 
Moreover, there is also a gap that concerns the educational level of the analyzed 
textbooks in the existing literature. Tajeddin and Pakzadian (2020) claim that most of 
the studies that have been conducted to analyze textbooks from an ELF or World 
Englishes perspective were at the tertiary, primary, and elementary educational levels. 
Thus, textbooks that are used in high school levels, particularly 12th grade, are still 
unexamined in both the Syrian and Turkish contexts. Yet, Luo (2024) argues that 
neglecting such a level leads to a loss within the developmental stages where learners 
conceptualize their identities as global users of English. Asakereh, Yousofi, and Weisi 
(2019) analyzed ELT textbooks that were used in high schools in Iran, which is in the 
Expanding Circle, and found out that such materials "do not provide sufficient

Additionally, due to the fact that ELF is generally regarded as a spoken practice,

comprehensibility and interpretability, for successful communication among 
multilingual and multicultural interlocutors." Therefore, a content analysis that 
examines the written discourse within the ELT materials is required to identify whether 
they contain these strategies for mutual understanding. 
 
All in all, the most important gap that needs to be filled is within the context of 
ELT in Syria. While there have been many conducted studies that examined ELF 
awareness in coursebooks between different countries, such as Guerra et al.’s (2022) 
comparative examination of both Portuguese and Turkish materials, the Syrian context 
is still uninvestigated. Despite the existence of studies that have been conducted to 
analyze MoNE-provided materials by Bay Halil (2019), Koçak (2021), and Öztürk 
(2024) in the Turkish context, it is completely unclear how ELT textbooks provided 
by the Ministry of Education of the Syrian government approach and reflect the 
worldwide expansion of English. As stated by Siqueira (2015), without investigating 
these locally produced materials, learners may stay in a "pedagogical Disneyland" (p. 
244) that does not totally match with their real-life experiences. Thus, a cross-national 
comparative content analysis research between Türkiye and Syria is needed since

 1.6. OPERATIONAL DEFINITIONS 
 
English as a Lingua Franca (ELF): refers to a communicative tool used among 
people who do not share the same linguistic as well as cultural backgrounds and for 
whom English is the only option for communication (Firth, 1996; Seidlhofer, 2011).  
 
Source Culture (SC): refers to learners' own or native culture (Cortazzi & Jin, 1999). 
According to the context of this research, it refers to Turkish and Syrian people, places, 
behaviours as well as values.  
 
Target Culture (TC): refers to the culture that belongs to Inner Circle countries like 
the United Kingdom and the United States where English is considered a native 
language of the population (Cortazzi & Jin, 1999). Any cultural reference to the UK, 
the USA, Canada, Australia or New Zealand was coded as TC. 
 
International Culture (IC): refers to diverse cultures from Inner, Outer and 
Expanding Circles where English has different types of status (Cortazzi & Jin, 1999). 
Operationally, any cultural reference to countries other than the learners' own country 
and other than Inner Circle countries was coded as IC. Examples include references to 
Japan, Egypt, Germany, China or Greece. 
 
Native Speaker (NS): refers to a speaker from an Inner Circle country such as the 
United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia or New Zealand (Matsuda, 
2002). 
 
Non-Native Speaker (NNS): refers to a speaker from an Outer or Expanding Circle 
country such as India, Singapore, Türkiye, Syria, Japan, Egypt or Germany (Matsuda, 
2002). 
 
Communication Strategies: refer to techniques used by speakers to overcome 
communication breakdowns and negotiate meaning in intercultural interactions 
(Vettorel, 2018; Yağar, 2020).

Expanding Circle: refers to countries where English does not have any official status 
but is taught and learned as a foreign language for communication (Kachru, 1985).  
 
Locally Produced Textbook: refers to a textbook that is written, designed and 
published by national authors and approved by the national ministry of education for 
use in state schools (Tajeddin & Teimournezhad, 2015). 
 
ELF Awareness: refers to the recognition and reflection of the global role of English 
as a lingua franca in ELT materials and practices (Sifakis, 2019).

CHAPTER II 
 
2. LITERATURE REVIEW 
2.1. INTRODUCTION 
This chapter provides a comprehensive review of the theoretical frameworks 
and empirical literature relevant to the core dimensions of English as a Lingua Franca 
(ELF) aware textbook analysis that guide the present research.  
 
To begin with, the chapter establishes the macro-level sociolinguistic context 
by elaborating on the historical global spread of English and the paradigm shift from 
English as a Foreign Language (EFL) to English as a Lingua Franca (ELF). Since this 
paradigm shift fundamentally challenges traditional monolingual approaches, it calls 
for an ELF-aware pedagogy that reflects the pluricentric reality of global 
communication (Seidlhofer, 2011; Sifakis, 2019). additionally, it discusses the 
established ideology of native-speakerism (Holliday, 2005) and its representations 
within English Language Teaching (ELT) materials. As argued by Kiczkowiak (2019), 
since native speakers are mostly represented as the only legitimate models within such 
teaching materials, the representation of non-native speakers is neglected, which is, on 
the other hand, leading to an inaccurate distinction. 
 
Furthermore, the chapter examines the issue of cultural representation in ELT 
textbooks, focusing on the dominance of Target Culture (TC) and the marginalization 
of Source (SC) and International Cultures (IC) (Cortazzi & Jin, 1999), in addition to 
the lack of cultural representation as conceptualized through Yuen's (2011) 4Ps 
framework. This framework is considered crucial because it highlights how textbooks 
often remain at a superficial 'tourist' level rather than fostering genuine intercultural 
communicative competence (Alptekin, 2002; Luo, 2024). Moreover, the 
representation of Native Speaker (NS) and Non-Native Speaker (NNS) representation 
in textbooks is explored based on Matsuda's (2002) framework. 
Finally, it addresses the role of communication strategies in ELF interactions 
(Vettorel, 2018; Yağar, 2020), with a particular focus on the critical absence of 
compensatory strategies. It must be stated that these compensatory strategies are 
increasingly recognized not as signs of linguistic deficit, but rather as proactive,

collaborative tools of meaning-making in intercultural encounters (Antonello, 2024; 
Vettorel, 2019). 
 
After the theoretical foundation is established, empirical studies from Asian, 
European, and Middle Eastern contexts will be reviewed systematically. After that, the 
focus is narrowed down to the context in Türkiye, then to the Syrian context, and 
finally to cross-national comparative studies. Due to the fact that cross-national 
comparative research between Expanding Circle countries reveals how different

2.3. NATIVE-SPEAKERISM IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING 
 
2.3.1. Native-Speakerism and English Language Teaching 
 
First of all, it should be noted that despite the emergence of the ELF concept, 
ELT materials and practices around the world remain heavily influenced by a dominant 
ideology known as native-speakerism (Kiczkowiak & Lowe, 2019; Öztürk, 2024). As 
defined by Holliday (2005, p. 7), this ideology is considered as an unconsciously 
established belief that "native-speaker teachers represent a superior 'Western culture' 
from which stem from the ideals both of the English language and of English language 
teaching methodology." Furthermore, due to the fact that this ideology is based on 
several problematic assumptions, it also impacts language teaching. For instance, 
English is considered as the cultural and linguistic property of its native speakers, 
which implies that only NSs have legitimate ownership of the language (Si, 2020; 
Widdowson, 1994). In addition to that, the native speakers are consistently regarded 
as the only legitimate authority on language correctness and the only target model that 
should be followed by language learners, while non-native speakers are at the same 
time viewed as inadequate or deficient learners (Cook, 1999; Kordia, 2015). 
 
Therefore, it must be stated that this perspective is deeply aligned with what 
Phillipson (1992) described as "native speaker fallacy"—the unfounded belief that

native speakers are automatically the ideal teachers and the only authorities of the 
language. Moreover, as demonstrated by Davies (2003), the concept of the 'native 
speaker' itself is regarded as an idealization that creates a false dichotomy, 
systematically ignoring the diverse range of competent multilingual speakers in the 
real world. 
 
Consequently, this ideology has been criticised as being both irrelevant and 
harmful for language teachers and learners. As argued by Holliday (2005), native-
speakerism can lead language learners to develop "language insecurity" and lose their 
confidence while using English. Due to the fact that this ideology fosters an 
unachievable goal of "passing" as a native speaker, it fails to develop competent and 
confident multilingual communicators (Cook, 1999, 2005; Seidlhofer, 2011). In 
addition to this, Cook (2007) emphasizes that the primary goal of ELT should be to 
help learners become successful "L2 users" independently, rather than trying to imitate 
an unrealistic, unachievable as well as impossible native model. 
 
For the present research, which examines state-approved textbooks used in two 
Expanding Circle countries where the majority of English teachers are non-native 
speakers, understanding native-speakerism is considered essential. This is due to the 
fact that the extent to which locally produced textbooks reinforce or challenge this 
ideology directly impacts both teachers' pedagogical choices and learners' 
communicative confidence. Kiczkowiak (2019) pointed out that native-speakerism is 
spread, normalized, and supported by powerful discourses that are evident in how the 
English language is presented in coursebooks. Lastly, by neglecting non-native 
speakers and failing to provide language learners with examples of successful non-
native users, it can be stated that textbooks reinforce this ideology, making their 
systematic evaluation from an ELF perspective an absolute necessity for this research. 
 
2.4. CULTURAL REPRESENTATION: FROM TARGET CULTURE 
DOMINANCE TO THE NEGLECT OF SOURCE CULTURE 
 
2.4.1. The Dominance of Target Culture and the Neglect of Source and 
International Cultures

First of all, it should be noted that Cortazzi and Jin (1999) distinguish culture 
types according to three main categories within ELT textbooks. These categories are 
structured as follows: Target Culture (TC), which refers to the culture of Inner Circle 
countries where English is spoken as a native language (e.g., the UK, the USA); Source 
Culture (SC), which refers to the learners' own culture; and International Culture (IC), 
which refers to cultures from a wide range of countries across the Inner, Outer, and 
Expanding Circles. Since this framework allows for a highly systematic examination 
of cultural references, it is considered as a fundamental tool for analyzing whether a 
textbook accurately reflects the global reality of English use or remains constrained 
within traditional, native-speakerist boundaries (Shin, Eslami, & Chen, 2011; Syrbe & 
Rose, 2018). 
 
From an ELF perspective, English is no longer regarded as the sole cultural 
property of Inner Circle nations, but it has become a global communicative tool 
(Baker, 2015; Seidlhofer, 2011). Consequently, since an exclusive focus on TC in ELT 
materials fails to prepare learners for real-world interactions, it is argued that they are 
far more likely to use English with other NNSs from diverse cultural backgrounds 
rather than with NSs (Matsuda, 2012; McKay, 2002). Similarly, Alptekin (2002) 
argues that the traditional "language-culture inseparability" argument was critically 
challenged, therefore, advocating for a balanced representation of SC and IC alongside 
TC in order to enable learners to maintain their own cultural identities while 
successfully engaging in international communication. 
Furthermore, the inclusion of SC in ELT textbooks is considered crucial due to 
the fact that it facilitates comprehension by making learning more relevant and familiar 
to learners. Ultimately, this approach fosters a strong sense of cultural identity for 
language learners who might otherwise feel severely excluded by representing foreign 
cultures (Cortazzi & Jin, 1999; McKay, 2002). In addition to this, as McKay (2012) 
and Guerra et al. (2022) explicitly highlight, the failure to respect and incorporate local 
cultures significantly neglects learners' familiar ways of doing things and meaning-
making. Consequently, this pedagogical negligence hinders their development of 
intercultural communicative competence.

However, despite this essential theoretical shift, it must be stated that a 
significant body of empirical research has revealed the predominant dominance of TC 
in ELT textbooks around the world. For example, Matsuda (2002) conducted research 
to analyse beginning-level Japanese EFL textbooks, she found an over-representation 
of Inner Circle cultures. This finding was later confirmed by Shin et al. (2011), who 
examined seven international textbook series and concluded that Inner Circle cultural 
content was overwhelmingly dominant in all of them. 
 
Besides, many recent conducted studies support that this established trend 
continues across the globe. For instance, Tajeddin and Pakzadian (2020) analyzed 
global textbooks and found a remarkable imbalance prioritizing Inner Circle cultures. 
Similarly, Syrbe and Rose’s (2018) study found that German English textbooks over-
relied on UK English models and static cultural depictions. In addition to this, in the 
Asian context, Luo (2024) conducted research and revealed that Taiwanese high 
school textbooks maintain the hegemony of American English and culture. It should 
also be noted that this hegemony is similarly evident in the Chinese tertiary context, 
where Liu et al. (2022) found an imbalance in representing Expanding or Outer Circles 
cultures by favouring Anglo-American cultures (as cited in Öztürk, 2024). 
 
On the other hand, recent comparative and local studies conducted in the context 
of Türkiye revealed findings that support this imbalance. As demonstrated by Guerra 
et al. (2022) and Öztürk (2024), both locally and internationally published coursebooks

multiculturality and pluricentricity of English in the modern era. 
 
2.5. REPRESENTATION OF NATIVE AND NON-NATIVE SPEAKERS 
IN ELT TEXTBOOKS 
 
2.5.1. Matsuda's Framework for Speaker Categorization  
 
Firstly, in order to analyze the ownership of English as presented in ELT 
textbooks, it is considered necessary for researchers to employ a systematic way to 
identify whether speakers and characters represented in the materials are native
26:
14 
 
speakers (NS) or non-native speakers (NNS). For this purpose, Matsuda (2002) 
developed a framework, which has been widely used in later textbook analysis 
research. According to this framework, English speakers who come from the Inner 
Circle countries, such as the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia, 
and New Zealand, are classified as NS; on the other hand, speakers who come from 
the Outer or Expanding Circle countries, like India, Singapore, Türkiye, Syria, Japan, 
or Germany, are categorized as NNS. Additionally, speakers who do not provide 
sufficient information about their nationalities are coded as "uncertain." 
 
Since this framework allows a quantitative evaluation of whether textbooks 
promote a native-speakerist ideology or integrate the demographic reality of ELF, 
where NNSs outnumber NSs, it is regarded as a crucial analytical tool. However, as 
Matsuda (2002) herself revealed in her research, a statistical analysis often reveals 
significant qualitative imbalance. Even if NNS characters are represented, they usually 
produce fewer words and are generally limited to secondary roles within the dialogues. 
As a result, this obviously means that the NNS hold only limited roles in the global 
use of English. 
 
2.5.2. Studies on NS/NNS Representation 
 
There have been a significant number of studies that have been conducted to 
examine the representation NS/NNS in ELT textbooks used in Expanding Circle 
countries and they generally revealing a reliance on NS characters. In their 
comprehensive analysis of global ELT materials, Tajeddin and Pakzadian (2020) 
confirmed this widespread bias by stating that widely distributed series consistently 
promote Inner Circle accents and native speakers as the primary target interlocutors. 
Furthermore, as a qualitative dimension to these imbalances, scholars critically 
highlight that when NNS characters appear in coursebooks, they are generally 
represented as "tourists" or visitors to Inner Circle countries—rather than being as 
legitimate as well as independent users of global English within their own contexts 
(Öztürk, 2024; Vettorel & Lopriore, 2013). In addition to this, Vettorel and Lopriore 
(2013) observed that these NNS characters are often given inauthentic, "fake foreign

accents" produced by native-speaker actors and fundamentally failing to provide 
authentic ELF exposure. 
 
On the other hand, in the context of Türkiye, recent empirical evaluations 
revealed findings that align with this native-speakerist orientation. To begin with, 
Koçak (2021) conducted research in order to analyse locally produced EFL textbooks, 
she found a significant dominance of NS characters. Similarly, Öztürk’s (2024) 
research revealed that locally produced Turkish EFL textbooks are monolingual and 
Inner Circle based, with a limited representation of NNS speakers. Additionally, Çam 
and Salt (2025) evaluated two global English textbooks used in Türkiye and found that

2.6. COMMUNICATION STRATEGIES IN ELT TEXTBOOKS FROM 
AN ELF PERSPECTIVE 
 
2.6.1. Communication Strategies in ELF Contexts 
 
Communication strategies have been defined as techniques used by language 
learners in order to overcome communication breakdowns when they lack necessary 
linguistic resources in the field of second language acquisition (Dörnyei, 1995; Faerch 
& Kasper, 1983). On the other hand, such strategies have a crucial role within the 
perspective of ELF. Since the speakers in ELF interactions do not share neither a 
common language nor cultural background, the ability to negotiate for meaning,
28:
16 
 
accommodate to other speakers as well as use compensatory strategies is considered 
more important than achieving native-like language proficiency (Cogo, 2009; 
Mauranen, 2012). 
 
Therefore, the aforementioned strategies are defined as "active tools of 
meaning-making" that help language learners to negotiate mutual understanding 
(Antonello, 2024; Vettorel, 2019). Furthermore, since ELF users are considered as 
speakers who rely on their "multilingual repertoires" according to this perspective, 
they use code-switching not as compensatory support for linguistic deficits, but rather 
as cooperative and accommodative moves in order to establish a shared frame of 
reference (Cogo, 2009; Vettorel, 2019). 
 
On the other hand, Vettorel (2018) and Yağar (2020) developed a typology that 
consists of ten different types of communication strategies (S1 to S10), such as S1 
(Negotiation of Meaning), S2 (Rephrasing), S3 (Clarification Request), S4 
(Confirmation), S5 (Appeal for Help), S6 (Correction), S7 (Fillers/Hesitation 
Expressions), S8 (Approximation), S9 (Circumlocution), and S10 (Code-switching), 
in order to systematically analyze these strategies in ELT materials. Additionally, 
compensatory strategies (S5, S8, S9, S10) are also regarded as particularly crucial for 
real-life ELF interactions due to the fact that they allow speakers to maintain 
communication even when facing lexical gaps. In addition to this, Dörnyei (1995) 
argued that these strategies are teachable, and it is stated that explicit instruction can 
significantly improve learners' ability to maintain communication in real-life 
situations. Moreover, scholars like Jenkins, Baker, and Dewey (2017) stated that 
integrating such plurilingual resources in ELT is considered essential because relying 
only on static native English norms fails to reflect the reality of how successful ELF 
users naturally practice English. 
 
2.6.2. The Compensatory Strategies in ELT Textbooks 
 
Despite their importance, Vettorel (2018) found in his research that ELT 
materials continue to present idealized, planned dialogues where communication takes 
place and systematically excludes compensatory strategies. Similarly, Yağar (2020)

17 
 
analyzed an ELT coursebook used in Türkiye and found that the most frequent 
communication strategy was Rephrasing (S2), while compensatory strategies (S5, S8, 
S9, S10) were completely absent. 
 
Furthermore, recent evaluation findings also align with this neglect. For 
instance, Katırcı and Karakaş (2023) revealed that coursebooks used in Türkiye 
primarily focus on basic turn-taking and minimal clarification, explicitly highlighting 
that the highly guided nature of these speaking tasks stands in direct contradiction to 
authentic ELF communication realities. In addition to this, this deficiency is also 
consistent with what Franceschi (2015) noted as scripted dialogues and audio materials 
in commercial coursebooks consistently fail to provide authentic examples of meaning 
negotiation among non-native speakers. 
As argued by Vettorel (2018), this absence is not merely a minor omission but 
reflects a deeper pedagogical problem, due to the fact that it creates a misleading 
impression that proficient English speakers do not face communication difficulties or 
need compensatory strategies. In reality, ELF Research has consistently demonstrated 
that even highly proficient speakers regularly use these strategies in order to achieve 
successful communication (Björkman, 2014; Cogo, 2009; Mauranen, 2012). 
Consequently, presenting an idealized, error-free version of English severely deprives 
learners of the opportunity to develop the necessary "strategic capability" in order to 
autonomously manage unpredictable cross-cultural encounters (Seidlhofer, 2011; 
Vettorel, 2018). On the other hand, no research was conducted to examine the 
representation of communication strategies, particularly the presence or absence of 
compensatory strategies, in a Syrian state-approved English textbook. Furthermore, no 
cross-national comparative research has also analyzed the strategy profiles (S1–S10 
frequencies) of 12th-grade English textbooks from Syria and Türkiye comparatively.

3.6. DATA ANALYSIS 
 
Hsieh and Shannon (2005) state that the directed content analysis can be used in 
theory as well as in framework-based studies to enable the researcher to identify 
patterns that are found in the data (as cited in Temiz, 2018). Hence, the data of the 
current research were coded based on the following theoretical frameworks: 
 
3.6.1. Cultural Representation Analysis: RQ3 
 
The cultural references within the textbooks were examined through integrated 
frameworks. To begin with, in order to identify the geographical orientation of the 
culture, Cortazzi and Jin's (1999) classification was adopted. Thus, the cultural 
references were coded as Source Culture (e.g., learners’ own culture. the Syrian or 
Turkish culture), Target Culture (e.g., the British or American culture), and 
International Culture (e.g., the culture of people who speak English as a foreign 
language such as Japanese, Syrian, and Turkish culture). Then, Yuen's (2011) "4Ps" 
framework was employed for the categorization of the cultural components. Hence, 
every type of the cultural elements was coded as Products (e.g., traditional foods or 
flags) Practices (e.g., social behaviours or daily routines), Perspectives (e.g., values of 
a group of people or their beliefs) and Persons (e.g., people who have important roles 
within their own society). Therefore, reading, everyday English, listening and some 
modules were examined within the 12th grade state distributed English student 
textbook in the Syrian context. On the other hand, MoNE distributed 12th grade English 
student textbook’s reading, listening transcripts, writing and speaking sections were 
analysed.

often avoid "risky" models. Secondly, the national curriculum guidelines of both 
countries may explicitly or implicitly Favor Inner Circle models. As stated by Kırkgöz

the Syrian context, since the 12th grade English textbook is designed and titled as

ELT materials. Hence, without any ELF based training, writers will certainly act 
according to their current experiences that themselves experienced as learners. Lastly,

Cultures" (EforSC) suggestion could be a better model to meet the local needs without

This research question was answered according to the frameworks provided by

represented different types of communication strategies. The rephrasing

Yağar’s (2020) analysis results of English textbooks used in the Turkish context.

compensatory strategies in ELT materials.

clearly in English, it can be taught through various exercises without exposing learners 
to diverse varieties. Additionally, the absence of important strategies like 
approximation, appeal for help, and code-switching may be due to the traditional ELT 
views of “lower-level” strategies, which consider them unessential competencies for 
language learners. Thus, it can be stated that this perspective reflects a dependency on 
native speakerism ideologies. However, Vettorel (2018) claimed that ELF research has 
also demonstrated examples of proficient speakers who use compensatory strategies 
to achieve successful communication. As a result, excluding them from English

6. CONCLUSION 
6.1. SUMMARY OF THE STUDY 
 
The present research examined locally produced 12th grade English textbooks 
used in Syrian and Turkish state high schools from an ELF perspective. A qualitative 
document and content analysis methodology was employed and supported by 
descriptive statistics. The analysed materials were the Syrian Ministry of Education's 
Emar series 12th grade English textbook and the Turkish MoNE approved 12th grade 
English textbook. The data were collected from reading passages, dialogues, exercises 
and visual content across all units and themes. Three theoretical frameworks were used 
for data analysis: Cortazzi and Jin's (1999) and Yuen's (2011) framework for cultural 
representation, Matsuda's (2002) framework for NS/NNS speaker identification, and 
Vettorel's (2018) and Yağar's (2020) typology for communication strategies. The 
following research questions guided the study: RQ1 (overall ELF awareness), RQ2 
(similarities and differences between textbooks), RQ3 (cultural representation), RQ4 
(NS/NNS speaker representation) and RQ5 (communication strategies). 
 
6.2. CONCLUSION OF THE FINDINGS 
 
 It must be stated that the overall findings of the current research unequivocally 
reveal that neither the Syrian nor the Turkish 12th-grade English textbook 
demonstrates adequate ELF awareness. This deficiency is primarily due to the fact that 
both instructional materials fundamentally fail to meet the necessary ELF criteria for 
cultural diversity (with IC ratios falling severely below 50%) and strategy diversity (as 
evidenced by the complete absence of compensatory strategies S5–S10 at 0%). 
Furthermore, it was observed that both textbooks share a strikingly strong orientation 
towards Target Culture (TC) dominance (56% each), while representations of Source 
and International Cultures remain severely limited. In addition to this, both materials 
heavily rely on Rephrasing (S2) as the most frequently utilized communication 
strategy (42% in the Syrian textbook, 56% in the Turkish textbook). Consequently, 
they completely lack the compensatory strategies that are considered essential in order 
to successfully navigate real-life ELF interactions. However, despite these shared

deficiencies, notable differences were found to exist between the two contexts. Firstly, 
due to its literary focus on international characters, the Syrian textbook presents a 
balanced, NNS-dominant speaker profile (59% NNS, 41% NS). Conversely, the 
Turkish textbook demonstrates a clear NS dominance (60% NS, 40% NNS), which 
strongly reflects traditional Turkish ELT policies that favor British and American 
models as standards to be followed. Secondly, it was determined that the cultural focus 
of the Syrian textbook is more person-based (17%), whereas the Turkish textbook is 
practice-based (55%). Moreover, digital communication contexts are represented far 
more diversely in Türkiye, while being limited in Syria. When evaluated according to 
Yuen’s (2011) 4Ps framework, it is evident that the Practice category (P2) dominates 
both textbooks (36% in Syria, 55% in Türkiye), while the Perspective category (P3) 
remains critically low (19% in Syria, 16% in Türkiye). Since this specific distribution 
exists, it indicates that both textbooks heavily focus on observable cultural behaviors 
rather than addressing the deeper cultural values required for an intercultural 
communication. In conclusion, it can be stated that both textbooks reflect a remarkably 
low level of overall ELF awareness; while the Syrian textbook shows some alignment 
with ELF principles regarding speaker balance, the English textbook in Türkiye is 
found to exhibit much stronger NS-centric tendencies. 
 
6.3. LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY 
 
The present research has several limitations that must be taken into account. 
First of all, the results of this research cannot be generalized to global English 
textbooks, materials or even other grade level because its analysis with restricted to 
two English textbooks from the Syrian as well as Turkish context. In addition to that, 
despite the presence of Teacher’s Book and students Workbooks, they were not 
analysed, thus the findings of the current research do not reflect the content of these 
supplementary materials. Moreover, even though ELF is regarded as a spoken practice, 
the present research focused mainly on written texts; reading passages, listening 
sections, dialogues, and speaking activities were examined. However, audio materials 
such as listening tracks were not analysed. Finally, due to the fact that this research 
examined textbooks as static documents, how English teachers use such textbooks 
withing the classroom context is uninvestigated.

6.4. SUGGESTIONS FOR FURTHER STUDIES 
 
 Based on the findings and limitations of the present research, the following 
suggestions for further research are proposed. Firstly, in order to provide a more 
comprehensive understanding of ELF awareness across secondary school curriculum, 
future research should focus more on other grade levels like 9th, 10th and 11th grades. 
Secondly, investigating how English teachers actually use these textbooks is also 
crucial in understanding their adaptations, thus future research should be classroom-
based. In addition, since these textbooks are designed and prepared locally, focusing 
on the perspectives of their writers, curriculum designers and policymakers is vital in 
understanding why they have Target Culture dominance. Cross-national comparative 
research can also be conducted in expanded contexts within the Expanding Cricle 
countries in addition to Syria and Türkiye to identify whether the findings of the 
current research reflect a boarder issue.  
 
6.5. PEDAGOGICAL IMPLICATIONS 
 
The current research provides significant pedagogical implications as well as 
insights for stakeholder like textbook, designers, curriculum developers, policymakers 
and teacher education programs. To begin with, a balanced distribution of Source, 
Target and International cultures should reflect the global use of English worldwide. 
Thus, vital communication strategies such as S5, S8, S9, S10 must be taught through 
authentic ELF interactions. On the other hand, the national curricula must integrate 
ELF-aware principles for better inclusion of cultural components, NS/NNS speaker 
varieties and compensatory communication strategies withing the textbooks.  In 
addition to that, pre as well as in-service English teachers also must be integrated into 
the process of designing ELF-aware pedagogy because, without ELF-based training 
they, as Alptekin (2002) argues, will continue to act based on their previous 
experiences as language learners.
